title: Fair for Whom?
outcome: By the end, I can compare group fractions and combine unequal-sized groups correctly.
scenario: A fictional badge reader is evaluated on bright and dim cards with known reference labels.
given: Version M is correct on 9 of 10 bright cards and 3 of 6 dim cards.
Version N uses the same cards: 8 of 10 bright and 5 of 6 dim correct.

steps.label: Discuss trade-off
steps.detail: N improves total and dim results but loses one bright success.

explanation: Adding correct counts and denominators weights each tested card once. Averaging 90% and 50% would incorrectly give unequal groups equal size in the all-card rate. The group breakdown reveals a trade-off hidden by the total. Decide what matters with the relevant users rather than announcing that one number proves fairness.

counterfactual.change: Give bright and dim groups equal weight as an explicitly different metric.
counterfactual.reason: This averages group rates and is not the original 16-card agreement rate.

student_task: Which group loses performance under N, and can total improvement erase that fact?
teacher_answer: Bright drops from 90% to 80%. No; retain the subgroup result alongside the improved total.
project_evidence: Report sorter outcomes by relevant conditions and record whose failures matter when choosing a revision.
limits: Six dim cards supply limited evidence; these descriptive rates do not prove a system is fair for all users.
review_note: New fictional worked case reviewed against the weekly topic and reserved independent assessment. Keep that assessment separate; this picture is supported practice.
